title: Role of Heat Treatment Atmosphere on the Microstructure and Surface Morphology of DLP-Fabricated High-Entropy Alloy Components.

recollection.starting_material: guess: DLP-fabricated “green” bodies consisting of a photocurable resin loaded with equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy powder
recollection.intervention: guess: post-print heat treatments at ~1000 °C for one hour under four different atmospheres (high vacuum, argon, nitrogen, and air)
recollection.structure: guess: development of a predominantly single‐phase FCC matrix with minor BCC precipitates; grain size grew from ~5 µm in vacuum to ~25 µm in air; a 1–2 µm surface oxide scale appeared in the air‐annealed samples
recollection.mechanism: guess: inert and vacuum atmospheres promote pore closure and normal grain‐boundary migration, whereas oxidizing environments drive surface oxide formation that pins boundaries and impedes diffusion
recollection.results: guess: vacuum‐treated parts reached ~99.5% theoretical density, average grain size ~15 µm, hardness ~320 HV; argon samples ~98.8% density and ~350 HV; nitrogen ~98.5% density, ~330 HV; air‐treated showed ~97.5% density due to oxide‐induced porosity and hardness ~300 HV

score.note: The recollection correctly contrasts oxidizing air with vacuum/inert conditions and identifies oxide formation as inhibiting diffusion and pore closure, matching a central mechanism. However, it gives the wrong alloy, adds nonexistent argon and nitrogen treatment groups, and misstates the heat-treatment schedule. Most structural details—FCC/BCC phases, grain sizes, and oxide thickness—are unsupported, though greater oxidation/porosity in air is directionally correct. All reported density, hardness, and grain-size numbers miss the actual oxygen/carbon contents, cracking behavior, transition temperatures, and strengths.
